code.title: Arrange-Act-Assert tests with Method_Scenario_Expected names

followUps:
One logical assert per test is the goal, but not necessarily one assert statement. A test should check one behaviour; several asserts that describe the same outcome (an order's status and total after checkout) are fine. If the first failing assert hides the others or the test needs a long name with 'and', split it.

Example: asserting result.Id, result.Name on one returned object is one behaviour; asserting a return value and an unrelated email being sent is two.

You usually do not test private methods directly; you test them through the public behaviour that uses them. A private method exists to serve a public one, so covering the public paths covers it, and tests stay valid when you refactor internals.

If a private method feels too complex to reach, that is a design hint: extract it into its own class with a public API and test that. Avoid reflection and InternalsVisibleTo as a habit; they lock tests to implementation details.

code.title: xUnit new instance per test vs NUnit shared fixture

followUps:
Use a class fixture, or a collection fixture when several test classes must share it. Both create the resource once and dispose it after the last test.

public class DbFixture : IAsyncLifetime { /* start container */ }
[CollectionDefinition("db")]
public class DbCollection : ICollectionFixture<DbFixture> { }
[Collection("db")] public class OrderTests { public OrderTests(DbFixture f) { } }

Classes in the same collection run sequentially, so shared state needs care. Cost: one start-up instead of one per class.

IAsyncLifetime lets setup and teardown be asynchronous. A constructor and Dispose cannot await, so starting a container, running migrations or opening a connection there means blocking calls.

Implement Task InitializeAsync() (runs before the tests, after the constructor) and Task DisposeAsync() (runs after). Use it on a test class for per-test setup, or on a fixture for per-class or per-collection setup. It avoids .Result deadlocks and hidden blocking.

code.title: Stub, fake and spy in one checkout test

followUps:
The London school (mockist) tests each class in isolation with mocks for all collaborators and drives design from the outside in. The Chicago school (classicist) uses real collaborators where cheap, fakes where not, and checks state and results.

London gives precise failure locations but couples tests to interactions, so refactors break them. Chicago survives refactoring better but a failure can point to several classes. Many teams mix: classicist inside the domain, mocks at I/O edges.

Do not read the clock directly; inject it. In .NET 8 use TimeProvider and in tests FakeTimeProvider, which you can set and advance.

var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2025,1,1,0,0,0,TimeSpan.Zero));
var svc = new Service(time);
time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31));
Assert.True(svc.IsExpired());

Before .NET 8 use your own IClock interface. Time-dependent tests then run instantly and never flake at midnight or across time zones.

Replace authentication with a test scheme, then send requests as different users and assert the status code. Add a handler that builds a ClaimsPrincipal from headers, register it in ConfigureTestServices, and keep the real policies.

Cases: no credentials gives 401, wrong role gives 403, right role gives 200. Example: X-Test-Role: Admin on DELETE /orders/5 returns 204, while Viewer returns 403. Testing through HTTP proves the policy is actually attached to the endpoint, which unit tests of the handler cannot.

Give each test its own data and clean up, so the order of tests never matters. Use unique ids or names (a new Guid per test), wrap each test in a transaction that rolls back, or reset tables with Respawn before each test.

If tests still touch the same rows, put those classes in one xUnit collection so they run one after another, or give each test class its own database or schema. Assert only on rows the test created, not on global counts such as 'the table has 3 rows'.

code.title: Why a naive in-memory store hides constraint bugs

followUps:
Make two contexts load the same row, change it in one and save, then save a change from the other and expect DbUpdateConcurrencyException. This needs a real relational database, since InMemory does not enforce tokens.

var a = NewCtx(); var b = NewCtx();
var p1 = a.Products.Find(1); var p2 = b.Products.Find(1);
p1.Price = 5; a.SaveChanges();
p2.Price = 6;
Assert.Throws<DbUpdateConcurrencyException>(() => b.SaveChanges());

The second UPDATE matches 0 rows because the row version changed.

A fresh DbContext has an empty change tracker, so it really queries the database instead of returning the objects the test just saved. With the same context, Find or a query returns the tracked instance, and the test can pass even if nothing was written correctly (for example a column that was never mapped).

Reading back through a new context proves the data reached the database and that mapping, conversions and defaults round-trip.

code.title: Change tracker states and what SaveChanges writes

followUps:
It stops tracking every entity and sets them all to Detached, without touching the database. In tests it lets you reuse one context while forcing the next query to hit the database instead of the cache.

ctx.Add(order); ctx.SaveChanges();
ctx.ChangeTracker.Clear();
var loaded = ctx.Orders.Find(order.Id); // real query

It is cheaper than creating a new context. It also helps in batch jobs to keep memory flat: clearing after every 1,000 rows stops the tracker growing with all of them.

A concurrency token (for example a rowversion column or [ConcurrencyCheck]) is added to the WHERE clause of UPDATE and DELETE. The change tracker keeps its original value from the query.

Example: UPDATE Products SET Price=6 WHERE Id=1 AND RowVersion=0x01. If another writer changed the row, 0 rows are affected, and SaveChanges throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException instead of silently overwriting. You then reload, merge or tell the user.

code.title: Lowest applicable version and downgrade detection

followUps:
Raise the direct reference to at least the version the transitive package needs, so the nearest declaration is no longer lower. If the direct reference is yours, change it; do not suppress the warning.

Example: you reference Lib 1.0.0, but Other 3.0 needs Lib 1.2.0. Change your reference to 1.2.0 (or the latest compatible one). If you cannot upgrade, pin an older Other instead. Suppressing NU1605 hides a build that would run with a version some package was never tested against.

It makes the versions listed in Directory.Packages.props also apply to transitive dependencies, so one central line pins them for every project. Without it, a central version only affects packages you reference directly.

Example: you list Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.3 centrally and set the property to true; an indirect use through some library is raised to 13.0.3 too. It is the clean way to fix a vulnerable transitive package for the whole solution.

Dependency confusion is an attack where someone publishes a public package with the same name as your private one, with a higher version, and the build downloads theirs by mistake. The attacker's code then runs on your build machines.

Defences: package source mapping (internal id patterns only from the internal feed), reserving your prefix on the public feed, and lock files with hashes. Example: map Contoso.* to the internal feed only, so a public Contoso.Utils 99.0 is never considered.

First find which package pulls it in (dotnet nuget why or dotnet list package --include-transitive), then update that parent if a fixed release exists. If not, add a direct reference to the patched version, or pin it centrally with transitive pinning enabled.

Example: App uses Lib 2.0, which depends on Json 12.0 (vulnerable); add Json 13.0.3 directly, then rebuild, run tests and check that audit warnings are gone. Note a reason in a comment so the pin is removed later.

code.title: MSBuild property evaluation order and global properties

followUps:
Props files are imported at the start of the project, before your own properties, so they hold defaults and settings. Targets files are imported at the end, after your project body, so they can read final values and add or override targets.

Put LangVersion or TreatWarningsAsErrors in Directory.Build.props, because the SDK reads them while evaluating. Put custom targets, or settings that must see what the project set, in Directory.Build.targets. If a props file reads a property the project sets later, it sees empty.

Define your own target that runs after Build with the AfterTargets attribute. It runs every time Build finishes successfully.

<Target Name="Notify" AfterTargets="Build">
  <Message Importance="high" Text="Built $(TargetPath)" />
</Target>

Use AfterTargets="Publish" to hook other steps, and Condition to run only in Release. Put it in the project or Directory.Build.targets.

Tag the fast tests and filter by the tag, so every commit runs only those and the slow ones run on a schedule or in a later job. In xUnit use [Trait("Category","Unit")].

dotnet test --no-build --filter "Category=Unit"

The alternative is to split projects (MyApp.UnitTests, MyApp.IntegrationTests) and run the unit project in the first stage. Integration tests then run in a parallel job after the quick gate passes.

Framework-dependent publish contains only your app and needs the matching .NET runtime on the machine; the output is small (a few MB). Self-contained includes the runtime (tens of MB) and runs on a machine without .NET.

Use framework-dependent in containers built on a runtime image and when the host patches the runtime. Use self-contained to control the exact runtime version, with -r linux-x64 --self-contained; add trimming or single-file to shrink it.

The most specific rule wins: a rule for one diagnostic id beats a category rule, which beats the dotnet_analyzer_diagnostic.severity default. A file closer to the source file overrides one higher up, unless the upper file says root = true and the closer one is silent.

dotnet_analyzer_diagnostic.severity = suggestion
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2007.severity = warning
[*.Tests.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2007.severity = none

Here CA2007 is a warning except in test files.

EnforceCodeStyleInBuild makes IDE-style rules (IDE0xxx, such as naming or var preferences) run during the command-line build, not only in the editor. Without it, dotnet build ignores them, so CI cannot fail on style problems the editor shows.

Set it to true in Directory.Build.props, set severities in .editorconfig, and a style violation configured as warning with TreatWarningsAsErrors fails the build. Cost: slightly slower builds.

code.title: Mutation testing: weak vs strong suite

followUps:
The compiler turns each async method into a state machine class with generated branches (null checks, completed-task checks, exception paths). These extra branches show up in the report as uncovered, even when every line you wrote is tested.

Example: a simple await repo.Save() may report 50% branch coverage because the already-completed path is never taken. Do not chase 100% branch there. Coverlet and ReportGenerator can exclude generated code with attributes such as [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]; judge by the behaviours you tested.

Stryker makes many copies of your code, each with one small change (a mutant), like >= to > or + to -, and runs your tests against each. If a test fails, the mutant is killed; if all pass, it survived and your tests do not check that behaviour.

The score is killed divided by total, for example 42 of 50 = 84%. It is slow, so run it on core modules or on changed files only (--since).

The outbox pattern writes the message to an Outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and a background publisher sends it later. Test three things against a real database and a broker container.

1) After the command, both the order row and one outbox row exist, and if the transaction fails neither does. 2) Run the publisher: the message reaches the broker and the row is marked sent. 3) Make the broker fail: the row stays pending and is retried, and the consumer handles a duplicate safely.

Start containers once and reuse them. A database or broker container takes a few seconds to start, so share one per test collection instead of one per test, and reset data with Respawn, which takes milliseconds.

Then run test classes in parallel across collections, split unit and integration into parallel CI jobs, cache NuGet packages and Docker images, and build once with --no-build. Example: 200 tests, one 10 s container start and 30 ms reset each is about 16 s, not 200 starts.
